issues.legal_issue: Regular occupation of a distinct part of rented premises by third parties for their independent professional practice, without adequate proof that the tenant retained control or that the arrangement was without consideration, constitutes subletting.
material_facts: The occupation of part of the rented premises by three medical practitioners was admitted.
The practitioners used individual cabins on a mezzanine floor to conduct their practices, and each had a separate telephone connection.
The tenant allowed the practitioners to practise there at regular intervals and permitted them to display their names and practice timings.
The Appellate Tribunal found that the practitioners had exclusive possession while practising and inferred that consideration had passed under the arrangement.
The High Court set aside the Tribunal’s eviction order after reassessing the evidence; the Supreme Court held that the Tribunal’s finding was not perverse.
issues.conclusion: The Tribunal’s finding of subletting was restored; the eviction ground based on subletting therefore stood established.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, subletting involves parting with possession to a third party without the landlord’s consent. Ram Murti Devi v. Pushpa Devi states that the landlord must prove a third party’s exclusive possession of all or part of the premises and monetary consideration; once parting with possession is established, the burden shifts to the tenant to explain. Flora Elias Nahoum v. Idrish Ali Laskar states that where the third party’s presence is admitted, the tenant must establish the nature and capacity of that presence. Bharat Sales Ltd. v. Life Insurance Corporation of India explains that direct proof of consideration may be difficult and that a court may infer it from proved facts, including delivery of exclusive possession.

predicates.eviction_proceeding_on_subletting_ground: A landlord seeks eviction on the ground that the tenant sublet all or part of the rented premises.
predicates.third_party_exclusive_possession: A third party occupies a distinct part of the premises to the exclusion of the tenant while using it for the third party’s own purposes.
predicates.monetary_consideration_reasonably_inferr: The proved circumstances support an inference that the tenant received or was promised consideration for allowing the third party to occupy the premises.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding alleges subletting, exclusive possession by a third party together with a reasonable inference of consideration means the subletting ground is established.

issues.legal_issue: A supervisory court may not overturn a fact-finding decision by reassessing the evidence when that decision is not perverse.
material_facts: The Appellate Tribunal reversed the Rent Controller’s dismissal of the eviction proceeding and found that the practitioners had been sublet part of the premises.
The High Court, exercising supervisory jurisdiction, set aside the Tribunal’s decision after examining the evidence and reaching a different view of possession and control.
The Supreme Court held that the High Court had entered the factual arena and reappreciated evidence, and that the Tribunal’s decision was not perverse.
issues.conclusion: The High Court impermissibly exercised supervisory jurisdiction as though it were an appellate court; its judgment was set aside and the Tribunal’s findings were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 of the Constitution confers supervisory, not appellate, jurisdiction over fact-finding decisions. A supervisory court may intervene where a finding is perverse, including where it results from non-consideration of material evidence, is contrary to the evidence, or rests on an inference impermissible in law; it may not simply reappreciate evidence and substitute its own view. The Supreme Court’s review under Article 136 in this appeal was limited to whether the High Court’s interference involved perversity or other error.

predicates.supervisory_challenge_to_fact_finding_or: A party challenges a fact-finding decision in a proceeding invoking a court’s supervisory jurisdiction.
predicates.tribunal_finding_not_perverse: The fact-finding decision does not disregard material evidence, contradict the evidence, or rely on an inference impermissible in law.
predicates.supervisory_court_reappreciated_evidence: The supervisory court reassesses the evidence and substitutes its own factual view for that of the fact-finding body.

issues.definition: In a supervisory challenge to a fact-finding order, if the finding is not perverse and the supervisory court reassesses the evidence, that interference is impermissible.
